newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian tariff hike harmful to economy - analyst.
newsitem.headline: Colombian tariff hike harmful to economy - analyst.

text.p: BOGOTA, May 30 Reuter - Colombia's recent decision to raise import tariffs clouds the outlook for pulling the country out of its current recession, a leading economic analyst said Friday.

Mauricio Cardenas, head of the private economic think-tank Fedesarrollo, said the higher tariffs, announced in March by outgoing Foreign Trade Minister Morris Harf, were negative in many ways, including the fact that they stimulated the country's booming trade in contraband goods.
The increase in tariffs, which vary widely in Colombia, was aimed at helping the government plug a gaping fiscal deficit, which totaled about four percent of gross domestic product last year.
But Cardenas, in an opinion column in Bogota's El Tiempo newspaper, said the move had done more harm than good because it added a new element of uncertainty to the business climate.

The move could still be blocked by Colombia's partners in the Andean Pact trade group, Cardenas said, adding that this, in turn, had prompted businessmen and industrialists to delay new investment decisions and the import of raw materials until they were certain that tariffs won't be cut again in the near future.
Finance Minister Jose Antonio Ocampo and President Ernesto Samper have refused to rule out a further hike in tariffs to cut a fiscal deficit that they see as a leading obstacle to growth.

But current Foreign Trade Minister Carlos Ronderos conceded, in testimony to the Senate Thursday, that higher import tariffs were "harmful to the economy" because they drove up local production costs and flew in the face of moves toward regional economic integration.

Cardenas stressed that higher tariffs also contributed to the artifical strengthening of the Colombian peso, since they reduce demand for dollars by importers. The peso's sharp run-up late last year hurt exporters badly since it increased the cost of Colombian goods abroad.
"Even from a strictly fiscal sense, you lose more through slower economic growth than you gain with higher tariffs," Cardenas said.
"What's worse is that the government has indicated the possibility of further increases in tariffs in the near future," he added.
